summary:
NASA Combustion Explorer transforms NASA’s complex combustion-science archive into an interactive research tool for spacecraft fire safety. We structured NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data across investigations, experimental runs, test matrices, publications, and source records, then connected it to our trained SPLADE neural sparse retrieval model for natural-language scientific search. 
SPLADE model helps retrieving the most relevant investigations or insights by taking the users input as search tokens. To make it more transparent, we implemented a feature "Splade Explorer" where the user can give an input, and then see the evaluation of the most important tokens to the model. This was the user can understand what words better to use to find the most relevant document and have a little hint about the models inner workings. 
The dashboard also shows experimental conditions  and curated fire-safety insights linked to source evidence, confidence levels, and caveats.
details:
NASA Combustion Explorer: SPLADE-powered retrieval over NASA PSI combustion investigations helps to make NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data easier to search, compare, and interpret.

Instead of manually searching for individual investigation pages, experiment tables, publications, and files, users can give an input in form of words or a filter and retrieve the most relevant NASA investigations and individual experimental runs.

The project uses a trained SPLADE neural sparse retrieval model. NASA PSI records are transformed into scientific chunks and encoded into sparse document vectors in advance. When a user submits their input, SPLADE encodes the query, compares it with the precomputed sparse index, ranks the most relevant records, and groups the results by NASA PSI investigation. The current retrieval corpus contains about 2,189 searchable chunks, including 1,862 experimental runs and 135 test-matrix records.


The intended impact is to reduce the time required to locate relevant evidence across decades of NASA combustion research. We also assume that our system will help researchers to encounter new information that they could have missed previously. Having a full overview of the research subject is very important, sometimes even more important than just saving time of searching for the right investigation or paper.

We developed the system using Python, Streamlit to stream the dashboard, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, SciPy sparse matrices, and pandas to build the model. The project is hosted publicly using Streamlit Community Cloud, with source code maintained on GitHub. The retrieval model and sparse index run directly with the application, so no generative-AI API is required at query time. The tests were made on our own CPU and then streamed through streamlit, the model was previously trained by us in another project! Some Sl tools helped us with writing the code and gathering some data for datasets due to the limited time (chat gpt, claude), but everything was rewived by us.

The creativity in this project is shown in the model we are using and the special splade exploration page. Splade and some other retrieveal models can be sensitive to the input, so we thought it was important for a person to see what tokens are most important for their search. This not only leaves the user with a basic idea of how does the dashboard even work, which is too, important, but also gives an idea on how to find even more relevant data.

Our team considered we considered data quality, missing experimental parameters, differences between investigation types, source traceability, model input limits, retrieval interpretability. Also at the start we had a problem with how to even make a proper dataset and spent some time on making proper database with research from PSI that would suit SPLADE. We made psi_id a key in the dataset, after this the info could be retrieved more consistenty.
